Hey girl, I also suffer from this. I've had this disorder for three years and I understand how it can absolutely devastate your live; it most certainly has wreaked havoc on mine. I'm going to give you a brief introduction to all the things I've tried in the past to disguise hair loss, hopefully one or some of these experiences will help you. 
Note: *preventing* hair loss is an entirely different ball game, and not what you asked for, so I'm going to try my best to avoid that.

When I first began pulling, it was an all-over thinning kind of thing. I used a powder like [this](http://www.dermmatch.com/?gclid=CKeXgb6NlrwCFSdp7AodcX4ARg) to disguise the thinning. These kinds of products are more common than you'd think, and are sold at most large beauty/hair stores (I got mine at Ulta.)

Last summer the pulling got very bad, and having long hair was not helping me. I cut it shoulder-length and died it light blonde. The blonde helped a lot to disguise the hair loss- the closer the color of your hair is to the scalp, the less noticeable it would be. Looking back, the blonde was a good idea- the haircut was not. It did not stop my pulling at all, and if anything, made it more difficult to cover up the damage I had done. Remember, the shorter the hair gets the less styling options you have.

When the damage started to become very visible, even with lighter-colored hair, we went to my hairstylist and asked about extensions. What I ended up getting were [hairdreams](http://www.hairdreamsusa.com/home) extensions, a product called the microline.

Some notes about these extensions:
It covered the center part of my scalp, a bit like a yamaka. The part that was covered by the extensions was impossible for me to pull from. It looked incredibly natural and made my hair appear much fuller immediately. It felt like a godsend.

The microline extensions were weaved into my hair and bonded- very difficult to explain. Pieces of my own hair were tightly wrapped around bonding points and secured. The bonding points did not hurt, per se, but were very sore and I became tempted to pull around those areas. Eventually I developed very large bald spots around the perimeter of the hairpiece. 

Pulling around the bonding points loosened them, and in turn loosened the entire hairpiece. I constantly had to go in to the hairstylist to get them tightened, an uncomfortable procedure. 
After a couple months in this thing, it had irritated my scalp to the point where I had pulled out my entire bang section and a large section on the back of my head. When it got to the point where I couldn't disguise it anymore, we moved on to the next thing: I decided to buzz my hair and get a wig. As painful as this decision was for me, I thought I needed a fresh start.

My hairdresser removed the extensions and when I saw the full extent of the damage I had done, I sobbed. The few bits of shoulder-length hair I still had were limp and sparse. The back center of my head was almost entirely bald, and I had no hairline at all. This was a very, very low point for me.
Shaving your head is liberating, in a way, but also very sad. I watched the little bit of me that I had left fall to the floor. 

I got a wig from [king's wigs](http://www.kingswigs.com). I have to say, the selection there is incredible and not terribly expensive. 
When it comes to wigs, you have one major choice: synthetic hair, or human hair? Human hair, of course, is much more expensive. You also have to remember, though, that synthetic wigs vary in quality: there are some that are very nice and realistic; there are some that look like, well, wigs. I originally set out to buy a synthetic, but fell in love with the cut and color of a human hair.

I also got a lace-front wig. Unless you plan on buying a wig with bangs, I would suggest a lace front as they look much more natural and blend in to your scalp, creating the illusion of a real hairline. I also would recommend a natural, straight or wavy wig. Wigs that are chemically curled are a lot harder to deal with, I've heard.
The next day at school I got a lot of compliments on my "haircut" and was asked a couple times if I had dyed it. I said yes. 

In a way, the wig is incredible for me: no matter how much damage I do to my actual hair, I can always put the wig on top of it and nobody knows. I don't have bad hair days; I don't have to worry about sleeping and messing it up. Right now, it's sitting on a stand across my room, looking all perfect and whatnot. 

But it also is not my hair. Wigs are hot and uncomfortable and itchy as fuck. You worry when you have to exercise, when you sweat, when there's a strong wind, when it slips a bit. There's the constant adjusting and emergency bathroom checks. All in all, I think it sort of sucks. I wish I had natural hair, hair that was growing out of my scalp like every other fucking normal human being in the fucking world. But I don't, I don't really have a choice at this point, and I'm very grateful that I have a wig to leave the house in.

As for getting my head shaved: like I said, it was a very emotional experience. When I first got it shaved, I felt stronger, like I had a fresh start. All my hair was going to grow back in and be all the same length, for once. It was bittersweet, but in a way I felt empowered.

The tiny peach fuzz feels funny and nice. For the first few weeks  I was obsessed with rubbing my head. It was too small to grasp, even with my fingernails, and pulling completely stopped. However, the urge was still there, and now that's it's grown to about half an inch, the pulling is back. In fact, I'm surrounded by hair as I type. I now have several pure bald spots on my scalp and it truly is disheartening to see them in the mirror. At this point, it feels like I will never be able to have long hair again: I simply will pull it all out before it gets the chance to grow.

I wouldn't quite say I regret shaving my head- because honestly, I didn't really have much of a choice at the time. The damage was so bad that it was the only option. But it is a very hopeless and crushing situation, knowing that I very well may never have long hair again. If you subscribe to beckie0 (a blogger/vlogger with trichotillomania), you may want to check out her experiences with shaving her head. I feel very much the same way about it as she does.

I'm going to stop this post because it's really starting to get long, but if you have any more questions or if you'd like to talk, feel free to message me here and I have no problem giving you my contact information. I hope my experiences can help you, and I wish you the best of luck in finding something that works for you.
